past_actions.summary: Volunteer two afternoons this week at Millfield Public Library, helping adults with basic computer literacy — email, video calls with family, navigating health insurance portals online.
past_actions.emotional_state: Settled and purposeful, with a low hum of background worry about health and mobility that I keep at arm's length through activity and routine. Not anxious. Not complacent. Something like cautious contentment.

past_actions.summary: Look up RoboRide Inc on the library computers Tuesday afternoon — not to make any decision, but to understand what the service actually involves. How does one summon a vehicle? What is the cost per ride? Is there an app required, and if so, is it the kind of app I can learn? I helped three people set up telehealth accounts last week. I can learn an app.
past_actions.emotional_state: Unsettled in a way I am choosing to treat as interesting rather than alarming. There is genuine unease — the 2am fear is real and I do not want to dismiss it. But there is also, underneath it, something I will cautiously call curiosity. I notice I am more open than I expected to be. I am watching that openness carefully, making sure it is genuine and not just me telling myself a story about being adaptable because I am afraid of being the kind of person who is not adaptable.

past_actions.summary: Download the RoboRide app on my phone this week — the library aide Marcus can help me if I get stuck — and book one short test ride. The destination will be the Millfield Community Center on Thursday afternoon, which I was already planning to walk to for the drop-in hours Lisa expanded. It is 1.4 miles. At $0.18/mile that is roughly 25 cents plus whatever base fare applies. I am not evaluating whether to give up the car. I am evaluating whether the app works, whether the vehicle is clean and safe, whether the wait is what they say it is, and whether I feel dignified at the end of it.
past_actions.emotional_state: Quieter than last tick. The unsettled feeling has not gone away but it has stopped being uncomfortable — it has become the texture of paying attention, which I recognize. The curiosity is no longer tentative. I am not performing openness. I am open.

past_actions.summary: Call Priya Sharma, my insurance agent neighbor, and ask a specific question: what would my monthly costs look like if I dropped the car — what happens to my auto insurance premium, and is there any renter or homeowner rider that would change? I am not telling her I am selling the car. I am getting information. I will also call the RoboRide customer line or check the app to confirm whether the service runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week — specifically whether a ride at 2am to a hospital emergency room is a thing I could actually book.

Formally adopt RoboRide as my primary transportation method going forward. Delete the mental category of 'trial' and begin treating robotaxi as my normal mode of getting around Millfield. Book a ride this week to the medical clinic for my routine blood pressure check — the appointment I would have previously driven to — as a deliberate first act of the new normal.

reflections.reflection: Five ticks ago I was sitting with a fear I had been carrying for years — that if I let go of the car, I would be letting go of the thing that stood between me and helplessness at 2am. That fear was real. I did not dismiss it; I examined it. I downloaded an app. I took a test ride. I called my insurance agent. I confirmed that RoboRide runs all night. And then I let it go. What surprises me now is not that I adapted — I always thought I could adapt — but how much room that fear was taking up. I look out now and see Millfield in genuine economic pain. Unemployment up. The spending index at 48. People I know by name are being laid off or closing businesses. Patricia Hawkins laid off people her father knew. Miguel is trying to retrain. Betty's diner is on auto row, which is ground zero. I had five ticks of internal work to do. That work is done. Now I look outward.
reflections.identity_shift: I no longer think of myself as a car owner who is experimenting with alternatives. I am a car-free person in a disrupted town who happens to have stable income, savings, relevant skills, and time. The 'retired' identity used to feel like it meant 'finished.' It does not feel that way now. I am not finished. I am available.
regrets: I spent tick 3 in pure routine when I could have been building something earlier. The disruption was already visible. I was watching it but not yet engaging it.

I have not yet had a real conversation with Robert Jackson, the rideshare driver in my contacts. He is being displaced by the very service I now depend on. I owe him at least an honest acknowledgment of that, even if there is nothing I can practically do about it.
successes: I took the car-free transition seriously and did it properly — not impulsively, not in denial, but by gathering real information and testing real assumptions. The 2am worry was addressed on its actual terms, not papered over.
I have maintained my library volunteer work through the disruption. That continuity matters. It kept me present in the community at the exact moment the community needed presence.
reflections.adaptation_notes: My archetype is 'adapter.' I now believe this is accurate, but the mechanism is slower than the word implies. I adapted not by being naturally flexible but by moving through genuine discomfort one small step at a time. The lesson I want to carry forward: the slowness is not weakness. It is how I verify that the adaptation is real and not just performance. What I need to watch: my normalcy bias is 0.79. High. That means I will tend to see the current state — my settled, car-free, volunteer life — as the new normal and may underrespond to the next disruption. I should deliberately ask, once a month, what I am not noticing.
